summary: Describes a way for hosts and gateways to send statistics data on request to a monitoring center or debugging host. Machines that wanted a remote statistics monitoring facility could implement it. It is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 996 describes a small request-and-response service for reading statistics from a remote host or gateway. The unit metadata marks the RFC Historic, and the RFC says the service is intended for casual monitoring and debugging rather than detailed machine analysis.

questions: what is the statistics server protocol
how to monitor hosts statistics remotely
subtitle: A lightweight protocol for requesting statistics from remote hosts and gateways.

tldr.problem: Remote monitoring through login or file transfer can be awkward and intrusive when operators need to inspect statistics regularly.
tldr.mechanism: A client sends a null-terminated ASCII command, and the server returns a null-terminated display-ready ASCII response.
tldr.outcome: RFC 996 defines a lightweight tool for casual monitoring and debugging, not a standardized full-function monitoring system; the unit metadata marks it Historic.

today: The unit metadata marks RFC 996 as Historic. The RFC describes STATSRV as a lightweight facility for casual monitoring and debugging.

sections.title: A Small Tool for Remote Checks
sections.content:
Hosts and gateways may record packet, error, and event counters for debugging and performance evaluation. Existing remote-login and file-transfer services can retrieve information, but the RFC describes them as awkward and intrusive for regular, frequent checks.

STATSRV is designed as a lightweight way to request these statistics with little intrusion into existing systems or networks. It is intended for casual monitoring and debugging, not detailed standardized reports for machine analysis.
sections.plainLanguage: STATSRV lets an operator ask another system for a short status report. It is meant for simple checks, not as a complete monitoring system.

sections.title: ASCII Commands and Responses
sections.content:
A client sends a null-terminated ASCII command to the server. The server replies with a null-terminated ASCII response that can be displayed on a printer or screen.

The RFC describes UDP as less intrusive and more efficient than TCP for this service. With UDP, each command and response must fit in one 576-octet IP datagram. The assigned port is 133 for both transports.
sections.plainLanguage: The client sends a short text command, and the server returns text that a person can read. The RFC favors a single UDP datagram for this lightweight exchange.

sections.title: Access and Security Limits
sections.content:
STATSRV does not provide access control or authentication. The RFC notes that a command could include a password or another measure to discourage casual misuse if needed.

The protocol exposes host statistics for monitoring and debugging, but the document does not define a standardized data model or detailed machine-readable report format.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol does not check who is asking for statistics. A site that needs a barrier against casual use would have to add a mechanism such as a password.
